lesson.grammar_point: the passive voice in institutional writing (be + past participle, agentless passive, by-phrase)

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: the standard wording that appears in every document of that kind and says nothing
to back a statement with evidence that a stranger can check
a weakness that an honest letter about you has to name
the first pass in which most files are removed without a conversation
to be given a job to do by somebody with the authority to give it
able to be checked by somebody who does not know you
a statement about yourself that the reader has no reason to believe yet
to put your own name behind somebody else's claim

paras: Before anybody speaks to a candidate, two readers spend about eleven minutes each with a file. Almost none of it is written in the voice a person would use out loud. The application was received. The file was reviewed. The headcount was verified. Nobody does anything in those sentences, and that is deliberate: the writer of an internal record is not a person, it is an office, and the register was built to sound that way. Most files are removed at this stage without a conversation ever happening, which means that the candidate is not rejected. He is overlooked, and the two are different failures with the same result.

The resume is written in the same register and for a different reason. Every line of a resume is a claim, and a claim is only a statement the reader has no reason to believe yet. Hard-working, dedicated, results-driven: all true, all boilerplate, and none of it can be checked by somebody who has never met you. What survives the screening is the line that can. Twenty-five employees and three sites is verifiable. In 2021 he was tasked with writing the pricing process down is verifiable, because there is a year in it and a thing that either exists or does not. The passive is doing real work in that sentence: the reader learns that somebody with authority handed him the job, without the writer having to name who.

Then there is the second letter, and it is the one that decides the file. A recommendation that praises everything is read as boilerplate and set aside, because a letter with no limit in it contains nobody's judgement. The letters that are believed do two things. They substantiate two or three claims with figures the office is able to check, and they name one real shortcoming and say what the candidate did about it. And once in the letter, usually only once, a name comes back after the word by: the turnaround was attributed to the site team. That sentence gives the result away on purpose, and it is the reason the reader believes the rest of the page.

bank.label: Say it naturally
items: The company was founded by my grandfather in 1974.
In 2021 I was tasked with writing the pricing process down.
Three projects are run at the same time, and each one is managed by a site engineer.
The turnaround was attributed to the site team, and it should have been.
Most of what I do now was not in the job I was trained for.
The figures can be vouched for by the client who paid them.

listenings.text: A file gets about eleven minutes from me on the first pass, and I want to be honest about what I am doing in those eleven minutes. I am not looking for the best written pages. I am looking for claims I can check. A resume that is all adjectives is boilerplate, and boilerplate does not get rejected, which is the part candidates never believe. It gets overlooked. Nobody in this office decides against it. It simply does not survive the screening, and no one ever writes down why. The sentences that make me stop have a number in them, or a date, or a name. Twenty-five employees. Three sites. In 2021 he was tasked with something specific, and here is what came out of it. A claim that can be verified is worth more to me than a claim that is beautifully phrased, and I would say that is the single thing I would tell every applicant if I were allowed to tell them one thing.

I have written maybe forty of these letters and I got the first ten of them wrong. I praised everything. I thought that was the job. Those letters are read as boilerplate and they are worth nothing, and the reason is simple once somebody explains it to you: a letter with no limit in it has nobody's judgement in it. If I say a person is outstanding in every direction, I have told you about my enthusiasm and not about him. The paragraph that gets believed is the one that names a real shortcoming and then says what he did about it. That paragraph is the reason the rest of the letter is believed at all, and I have watched it work. One more thing, on who to ask. People chase the most senior name they can reach. Do not. Ask somebody who can vouch for a specific result with figures in front of them. Seniority with no detail reads as a favour, and everybody on the other side of the desk knows it.
